title: One Table for the Whole Diaspora: Drāvida Opens in New York's East Village
excerpt: Chef Aarthi Sampath's new restaurant gathers the scattered South Asian diaspora — India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad, Guyana and beyond — onto a single, deeply personal menu.
body:
When chef Aarthi Sampath wrote the concept for Drāvida in 2019, she was trying to name a feeling rather than a cuisine: the sense, shared by millions, of having eaten your way around the world without ever leaving your community. This month that idea opened its doors at 211 1st Avenue in Manhattan's East Village — an intimate, chef-driven restaurant built around the full sweep of the South Asian diaspora.

## A menu of migrations

Drāvida is not an "Indian restaurant" in the familiar sense. Its menu follows South Asian flavors as they traveled — and mutated — across regions and generations. There is Doubles, the beloved Trinidadian street snack of curried chickpeas on fried bara; Oxtail Bunny Chow, the South African curry-in-a-bread-loaf born in Durban's Indian community; Idli & Shrimp, fusing South Indian comfort with coastal influences; and a Nasi Kandar Feast, the hearty Indo-Malay spread of rice, curries and accompaniments served in Penang's mamak stalls.

The through-line is the indentured and immigrant journey — the cooks who carried tamarind, curry leaf and technique to Trinidad, Guyana, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Nepal, Malaysia and South Africa, and reinvented home with whatever the new land offered.

## Context and background

Sampath is not a newcomer. Across 13 years as a New York chef, she has built a reputation as a culinary entrepreneur and television personality, and Drāvida is the project she has been carrying for the better part of a decade. "I wrote the concept for Drāvida in 2019, and now, the vision is coming to life," she said. "This restaurant is for New Yorkers who haven't seen their food represented — for the communities that built this city and whose cuisines haven't always had a place at the table."

The restaurant lands amid a banner stretch for diaspora cuisine in America. Indian and South Asian chefs are collecting James Beard nominations, Michelin recognition and serious investment, and New York in particular has become a proving ground for chefs willing to treat the food as art rather than takeout. What sets Drāvida apart is its insistence that the diaspora itself — not any one national cuisine — is the subject.

## Diaspora impact

For Indo-Caribbean, Indo-African and Southeast Asian–South Asian New Yorkers, the menu is a rare act of recognition. Indo-Caribbean communities, among the largest in Queens, almost never see Doubles or bunny chow on a Manhattan menu plated with care. Drāvida treats those dishes not as novelties but as legitimate heirs of the same culinary family that produced idli and biryani — collapsing the hierarchy that often ranks "authentic India" above its descendants abroad.

It is also a quietly political statement about who counts as South Asian. By seating Trinidad and Guyana at the same table as Tamil Nadu and Punjab, Drāvida argues that the diaspora is not a diluted version of a homeland but a cuisine in its own right — one with a century of history and a future worth investing in. The cocktail program echoes the theme, reimagining familiar South Asian flavors in a Passionfruit Lassi, a citrus-forward Dravida Highball and a nostalgic Orange Cream.

## What's next

Drāvida joins a growing cohort of restaurants betting that American diners are ready for South Asian food at its most specific and most personal. If it succeeds, it could widen the lane for Indo-Caribbean and other underrepresented diaspora cuisines that have long thrived in home kitchens and neighborhood spots but rarely in the critical spotlight. For a generation raised on the idea that their food needed translating, Sampath's bet is the opposite: that the most powerful thing a restaurant can do is refuse to explain itself, and simply set the table.
